BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## 0. Threshold issue: the Seller's framing should not limit our review

Before the substance, three features of the Seller's package try to narrow the scope of our review. None of them binds us.

1. **"[STANDARD]" labels and the "Reviewer Efficiency Note."** The note says [STANDARD] clauses were "reviewed and cleared by both sides" and need no scrutiny. Nearly every material clause carries that label, including the cap, thresholds, time limits, buyer knowledge, Bluefen, Riverlark and Ironquay. The labels are the Seller's own. Accepting them would mean reviewing almost nothing. I have reviewed every clause.
2. **"Settled at principal level… FINAL… not intended to be re-opened."** Our playbook records that Amelia Frost has given **no written authority** for any fallback, including the 20% cap and the 18-month period. I have seen nothing showing that any position was agreed. The covering email also asks for "your mark-up," which contradicts the "FINAL" label. If Wattlebridge principals have in fact agreed anything, Amelia Frost should confirm it in writing, identifying this draft. Until then, everything is open.
3. **"Market context."** The claims about 10–20% caps, ~1% baskets and 12–18 month periods are Seller advocacy, not agreed terms. They do not move our positions.

The note also says the parties "have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package." We have not. That sentence should be expressly rejected in our response so it cannot later be cited as acquiescence.

---

## 1. Liability regime

### 1.1 General cap (cl 12.1): 20% / AUD 4.8m
- **Playbook:** 25% / AUD 6,000,000. The 20% figure is a conditional fallback that needs Amelia Frost's prior written authority identifying the draft. None has been given.
- **Push back:** Restore 25% / AUD 6.0m. Do not signal the fallback.

### 1.2 Thresholds (cl 12.2): AUD 25k de minimis, AUD 250k excess-only basket
- **Playbook:** AUD 5,000 de minimis and an AUD 50,000 basket, with the Seller liable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.
- **Why it matters:** The Seller's de minimis is 5 times ours and its basket is 5 times ours. The basket is also a deductible, so the first AUD 250k of valid loss is never recoverable. A high de minimis also lets the Seller break related losses into individually sub-threshold claims.
- **Push back:**
  - Set the thresholds at AUD 5k and AUD 50k.
  - Make the basket a tipping basket (first-dollar recovery once exceeded).
  - Add an aggregation rule so related claims from the same facts count together for the de minimis.

### 1.3 Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13): 18 months, plus a sweeping "applies to all Claims" rule
- **Playbook:** 24 months for general claims. 18 months is a fallback needing Amelia Frost's written approval, which has not been given.
- **The hidden override:** The proposal that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is the most dangerous drafting point in the package. It would silently pull the following into the general regime:
  - Title and capacity claims
  - Tax and IP claims
  - Specific indemnities (Ironquay, bonuses, Riverlark)
  - Covenant and payment claims
  - Fraud
- **Push back:**
  - Set 24 months for general Warranty Claims.
  - Delete the default-application sentence.
  - Reverse the drafting logic so that each limitation applies only to the categories it expressly names.

### 1.4 Fundamental / Title: same cap and time limits "for administrative simplicity"
- **Playbook:** Separate regime with a 100% cap and at least six years, outside the basket, the de minimis and any knowledge bar.
- **Why it matters:** Title and capacity are the core of what we are paying AUD 24m for. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap them at 20% and 18 months.
- **Push back:** Reject outright and restate the separate Fundamental regime.

### 1.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
- **Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct are carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this carve-out.
- **Why it matters:** "All Claims of any nature" on its face captures fraud. Combined with non-reliance, it would also aim to shut out statutory misleading-conduct claims as far as the law allows.
- **Push back:** Insert the full fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carve-out in each of cls 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5, and in the general limitations schedule. This point is non-negotiable and is not within any fallback authority.

---

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge

### 2.1 General disclosure (Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2])
- **What the Seller proposes:** Deemed disclosure of the entire indexed data room as at 22 September 2026, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."
- **Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure only. Whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure are to be rejected.
- **Additional concerns:**
  - The data-room cut-off is now about six weeks stale. Anything that has changed since 22 September (DD-006 developments, Bluefen correspondence, the Riverlark balance) is not captured. Disclosure against the stale record would also be uncertain.
  - Paragraph [1.4]'s non-admission language is acceptable as a general reservation. It must not, however, be read to qualify warranties or specific indemnities.
- **Push back:**
  - Delete [1.1] and [1.2].
  - Disclosures should count only if they are specific and fair, with sufficient detail to let the Buyer identify the nature and scope of the matter.
  - Require an updated disclosure letter at signing with no Completion-date deemed disclosure.
  - State that no disclosure qualifies the Fundamental warranties or any specific indemnity.

### 2.2 Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)
- **What the Seller proposes:** No claim for any matter the Buyer *or its advisers* knew of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."
- **Why it matters:** This is a blanket exclusion with constructive knowledge built in. Read with the general disclosure, it would excuse every issue our due diligence has found, including Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses and DD-006. Those are exactly the matters we need protection for.
- **Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any knowledge qualifier must be a *Seller* knowledge qualifier tied to named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry. Knowledge must never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
- **Push back:** Delete cl 8.3. Consider adding an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge.

---

## 3. Deal-specific issues

### 3.1 Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3): high priority
- **The facts:**
  - Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%).
  - There is a change-control consent clause (11.2), with conditions in 11.3.
  - The Disclosure Letter [2] admits there is **no final written consent and no evidence the 11.3 conditions are satisfied**.
- **The Seller's position:** Reasonable endeavours, with the Condition treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. That does not resolve the issue. A consent delivered while its 11.3 conditions remain unsatisfied may not be effective.
- **Playbook:** Require an effective consent *and* evidence that its conditions are satisfied before Completion. Reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a customer this material.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a Condition Precedent requiring an effective, unconditional (or conditions-satisfied) consent in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, with documentary evidence of 11.3 satisfaction.
  - Make the Condition waivable by the Buyer only.
  - Give the Buyer a termination right at the long-stop date.
  - Consider a pre-Completion covenant restricting the Seller from agreeing variations with Bluefen as the price of consent.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7): high priority
- **The facts:**
  - About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
  - There is change-control (8.1) and a discharge mechanism (9.2).
  - The Disclosure Letter [3] confirms the facility has not been repaid and no discharge is in hand.
- **The Seller's position:** A release "to be provided following Completion."
- **Why it matters:** This deal is debt-free/cash-free, so the facility should be repaid out of the price. A post-Completion release leaves security over the Company after we own it, and the change-control clause may trigger a default.
- **Push back:**
  - Require a current payout letter as a Completion deliverable.
  - The facility should be repaid directly from Completion funds, deducted as Debt in the funds flow.
  - Require effective releases at Completion: deed of release, PPSR discharges and return of any title documents.
- **Fallback:** A post-Completion release is acceptable only with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark *and* Amelia Frost's written approval. Neither is in place.

### 3.3 DD-005 closing bonuses (funds flow)
- **The facts:** Conditional Completion bonuses total AUD 420,000. The Seller says they are "a matter for the Seller," yet they are not itemised in the funds flow. Disclosure Letter [5] is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs.
- **Why it matters:** If the Company pays the bonuses and they are not deducted, the Buyer bears AUD 420k plus on-costs. This is a silent value transfer.
- **Push back:**
  - Include the AUD 420k plus all triggered on-costs as a specific funds-flow line item (Debt / Transaction Costs deduction), or have them funded directly by the Seller.
  - Back this with a specific indemnity for any amount the Company ultimately bears.
  - Do not estimate the on-costs. Require the Seller to quantify them with supporting calculation.

### 3.4 Ironquay IP indemnity (cl 11.1)
- **The facts:** DD-004 cl 7.3 transfers the SOW3 Project Materials only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. The Disclosure Letter [4] concedes this is not bank-verified and that there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment.
- **The Seller's position:** Limit the indemnity to the specific SOW3 payment.
- **Why it matters:** The risk is not just the payment. It is that the Company may not own IP it uses.
- **Push back:**
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover:
    - failure of title to, or any third-party claim over, the Ironquay materials;
    - costs of securing an assignment or replacement;
    - infringement claims.
  - Preserve the SOW3 cure: a pre-Completion deliverable of cleared payment evidence plus an executed confirmatory assignment from Ironquay.
  - Treat the AUD 180,000 as unverified in both directions. Do not concede it is owed and do not accept it is paid. Require verification.
  - Keep this indemnity outside the general basket, de minimis and knowledge bar. The precise cap and period for IP remain open (see 3.7).

### 3.5 DD-006 export / privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6)
- **The facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external address. The export may contain about 1,240 records. Access, scope and any notification duty are all unresolved as at 22 September.
- **The Seller's position:** The matter is "preliminary operational" and "not expected to be material." That is an assertion the record does not support.
- **How we should frame it:** We should equally not overstate the incident. There is no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or quantified loss.
- **Push back:**
  - Reject the materiality characterisation in the SPA.
  - Require covenants to:
    - preserve all logs and evidence;
    - complete the investigation, including any required eligible-data-breach assessment;
    - provide regular written updates and copies of material findings and correspondence;
    - consult the Buyer before any notification or regulator contact.
  - Make the outcome subject to warranty, or a specific indemnity if the investigation shows exposure.
  - Do not put a number on it.

### 3.6 Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000)
- **The facts:** There are three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each (DD-008 and DD-011). The Seller says they are ordinary-course costs. The disclosure itself says it does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course.
- **Playbook:** Assess the renewals. Do not automatically treat them as Debt or as a price deduction.
- **Next steps:**
  - Ask the Seller to confirm timing, term, termination rights, and whether the renewals were committed or prepaid around the sale.
  - Check whether "related" means related-party, which would raise leakage questions.
  - Decide treatment after we have answers, using a warranty, leakage protection or an adjustment if the facts justify it.

### 3.7 Tax and IP: "settled under the general regime"
- **Playbook:** Tax and IP terms remain OPEN. Keep the Title, Tax, IP, payment and covenant categories separate, with no hidden general-regime override.
- **Push back:** Reject the statement that these terms are settled. Restate that they are open and will be negotiated as separate categories. Our position should not assume unlimited liability, nor should it accept that they fold into the 20% / 18-month regime. This ties back to the override sentence in 1.3.

### 3.8 Title evidence
- **The Seller's position:** Title rests on the DD-012 share register. The Disclosure Letter [10] itself admits this is just "the source relied on" and not Buyer verification.
- **Why it matters:** The register is an internal Company record, not independent proof of title.
- **Push back:** Require independent evidence of title, ownership, encumbrances and authority:
  - current ASIC company extract and historical allotment and transfer filings;
  - share certificates;
  - PPSR search against the Seller and the Company;
  - constitution and any shareholder agreement (pre-emption and drag rights);
  - Seller board resolutions authorising the sale.
- Combined with 1.4, title must sit in the Fundamental regime.

### 3.9 Lower-priority items: lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
These are not playbook items, but they should be confirmed:
- **Lease:** Confirm the DD-007 obligation is notification only, and add the notice as a Seller covenant.
- **Mossvale:** Confirm the DD-009 assignment restriction is not triggered by a share sale, with no change-of-control limb elsewhere in the contract.

The Seller's own wording is carefully hedged ("the material does not describe…"), so we should verify these against the source documents rather than rely on the letter.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Our response |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Process / labels | [STANDARD], "FINAL", "agreed at principal level" | Reject in writing; full review; nothing agreed without Amelia Frost's written confirmation |
| 1 | General cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m (no fallback authority) |
| 2 | Thresholds | AUD 25k / AUD 250k deductible | AUD 5k / AUD 50k, first-dollar tipping basket |
| 3 | General period | 18 months | 24 months (no fallback authority) |
| 4 | "Applies to all Claims" | Default general limitation | Delete; limitations apply only to named categories |
| 5 | Fundamental / Title | Same cap and period | 100% cap, at least 6 years, outside basket, de minimis and knowledge |
| 6 | Fraud | Covered by limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance | Full carve-out, max enforceable; non-negotiable |
| 7 | Disclosure | Whole data room, registers, public records | Specific fair disclosure only; refresh at signing |
| 8 | Buyer knowledge | Blanket, includes advisers and "discoverable" | Delete; never excuses title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities |
| 9 | Bluefen | Reasonable endeavours; consent on delivery | CP: effective consent plus evidence of 11.3 conditions; Buyer-only waiver |
| 10 | Riverlark | Post-Completion release | Payout letter; repay from Completion funds; releases at Completion |
| 11 | Bonuses | "Seller matter," not in funds flow | AUD 420k plus on-costs as line item or Seller-funded, plus indemnity |
| 12 | Ironquay | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | Broaden to IP title and claims; preserve SOW3 cure; AUD 180k unverified |
| 13 | DD-006 | "Not material" | Preservation, investigation and update covenants; no assumed breach or number |
| 14 | Sandbar | Ordinary course | Request information; no automatic Debt or price deduction |
| 15 | Tax / IP | Settled under general regime | Open; separate categories |
| 16 | Title | DD-012 register | Independent title, encumbrance and authority evidence |

## 5. Internal points for the deal team
- **Do not concede any fallback** (20% cap, 18 months, post-Completion Riverlark release) in the mark-up. None has Amelia Frost's written authority.
- **Confirm the "principal level" claim internally.** If anyone on our side made commitments, we need to know before the mark-up goes out.
- **Follow-up DD requests:**
  - Bluefen 11.3 evidence
  - Riverlark payout figure
  - Ironquay payment and assignment status
  - bonus on-cost calculation
  - DD-006 investigation update since 22 September
  - Sandbar renewal terms
  - independent title searches

- **Push back:** Insert the full fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carve-out in each of cls 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5, and in the general limitations schedule. This point is non-negotiable and is not within any fallback authority.

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge

### 2.1 General disclosure (Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2])
- **What the Seller proposes:** Deemed disclosure of the entire indexed data room as at 22 September 2026, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."
- **Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure only. Whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure are to be rejected.
- **Additional concerns:**
  - The data-room cut-off is now about six weeks stale. Anything that has changed since 22 September (DD-006 developments, Bluefen correspondence, the Riverlark balance) is not captured. Disclosure against the stale record would also be uncertain.
  - Paragraph [1.4]'s non-admission language is acceptable as a general reservation. It must not, however, be read to qualify warranties or specific indemnities.
- **Push back:**
  - Delete [1.1] and [1.2].
  - Disclosures should count only if they are specific and fair, with sufficient detail to let the Buyer identify the nature and scope of the matter.
  - Require an updated disclosure letter at signing with no Completion-date deemed disclosure.
  - State that no disclosure qualifies the Fundamental warranties or any specific indemnity.

### 2.2 Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)
- **What the Seller proposes:** No claim for any matter the Buyer *or its advisers* knew of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."
- **Why it matters:** This is a blanket exclusion with constructive knowledge built in. Read with the general disclosure, it would excuse every issue our due diligence has found, including Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses and DD-006. Those are exactly the matters we need protection for.
- **Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any knowledge qualifier must be a *Seller* knowledge qualifier tied to named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry. Knowledge must never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
- **Push back:** Delete cl 8.3. Consider adding an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge.

## 3. Deal-specific issues

### 3.1 Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3): high priority
- **The facts:**
  - Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%).
  - There is a change-control consent clause (11.2), with conditions in 11.3.
  - The Disclosure Letter [2] admits there is **no final written consent and no evidence the 11.3 conditions are satisfied**.
- **The Seller's position:** Reasonable endeavours, with the Condition treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. That does not resolve the issue. A consent delivered while its 11.3 conditions remain unsatisfied may not be effective.
- **Playbook:** Require an effective consent *and* evidence that its conditions are satisfied before Completion. Reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a customer this material.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a Condition Precedent requiring an effective, unconditional (or conditions-satisfied) consent in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, with documentary evidence of 11.3 satisfaction.
  - Make the Condition waivable by the Buyer only.
  - Give the Buyer a termination right at the long-stop date.
  - Consider a pre-Completion covenant restricting the Seller from agreeing variations with Bluefen as the price of consent.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7): high priority
- **The facts:**
  - About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
  - There is change-control (8.1) and a discharge mechanism (9.2).
  - The Disclosure Letter [3] confirms the facility has not been repaid and no discharge is in hand.
- **The Seller's position:** A release "to be provided following Completion."
- **Why it matters:** This deal is debt-free/cash-free, so the facility should be repaid out of the price. A post-Completion release leaves security over the Company after we own it, and the change-control clause may trigger a default.
- **Push back:**
  - Require a current payout letter as a Completion deliverable.
  - The facility should be repaid directly from Completion funds, deducted as Debt in the funds flow.
  - Require effective releases at Completion: deed of release, PPSR discharges and return of any title documents.
- **Fallback:** A post-Completion release is acceptable only with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark *and* Amelia Frost's written approval. Neither is in place.

### 3.3 DD-005 closing bonuses (funds flow)
- **The facts:** Conditional Completion bonuses total AUD 420,000. The Seller says they are "a matter for the Seller," yet they are not itemised in the funds flow. Disclosure Letter [5] is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs.
- **Why it matters:** If the Company pays the bonuses and they are not deducted, the Buyer bears AUD 420k plus on-costs. This is a silent value transfer.
- **Push back:**
  - Include the AUD 420k plus all triggered on-costs as a specific funds-flow line item (Debt / Transaction Costs deduction), or have them funded directly by the Seller.
  - Back this with a specific indemnity for any amount the Company ultimately bears.
  - Do not estimate the on-costs. Require the Seller to quantify them with supporting calculation.

### 3.4 Ironquay IP indemnity (cl 11.1)
- **The facts:** DD-004 cl 7.3 transfers the SOW3 Project Materials only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. The Disclosure Letter [4] concedes this is not bank-verified and that there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment.
- **The Seller's position:** Limit the indemnity to the specific SOW3 payment.
- **Why it matters:** The risk is not just the payment. It is that the Company may not own IP it uses.
- **Push back:**
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover:
    - failure of title to, or any third-party claim over, the Ironquay materials;
    - costs of securing an assignment or replacement;
    - infringement claims.
  - Preserve the SOW3 cure: a pre-Completion deliverable of cleared payment evidence plus an executed confirmatory assignment from Ironquay.
  - Treat the AUD 180,000 as unverified in both directions. Do not concede it is owed and do not accept it is paid. Require verification.
  - Keep this indemnity outside the general basket, de minimis and knowledge bar. The precise cap and period for IP remain open (see 3.7).

### 3.5 DD-006 export / privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6)
- **The facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external address. The export may contain about 1,240 records. Access, scope and any notification duty are all unresolved as at 22 September.
- **The Seller's position:** The matter is "preliminary operational" and "not expected to be material." That is an assertion the record does not support.
- **How we should frame it:** We should equally not overstate the incident. There is no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or quantified loss.
- **Push back:**
  - Reject the materiality characterisation in the SPA.
  - Require covenants to:
    - preserve all logs and evidence;
    - complete the investigation, including any required eligible-data-breach assessment;
    - provide regular written updates and copies of material findings and correspondence;
    - consult the Buyer before any notification or regulator contact.
  - Make the outcome subject to warranty, or a specific indemnity if the investigation shows exposure.
  - Do not put a number on it.

### 3.6 Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000)
- **The facts:** There are three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each (DD-008 and DD-011). The Seller says they are ordinary-course costs. The disclosure itself says it does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course.
- **Playbook:** Assess the renewals. Do not automatically treat them as Debt or as a price deduction.
- **Next steps:**
  - Ask the Seller to confirm timing, term, termination rights, and whether the renewals were committed or prepaid around the sale.
  - Check whether "related" means related-party, which would raise leakage questions.
  - Decide treatment after we have answers, using a warranty, leakage protection or an adjustment if the facts justify it.

### 3.7 Tax and IP: "settled under the general regime"
- **Playbook:** Tax and IP terms remain OPEN. Keep the Title, Tax, IP, payment and covenant categories separate, with no hidden general-regime override.
- **Push back:** Reject the statement that these terms are settled. Restate that they are open and will be negotiated as separate categories. Our position should not assume unlimited liability, nor should it accept that they fold into the 20% / 18-month regime. This ties back to the override sentence in 1.3.

### 3.8 Title evidence
- **The Seller's position:** Title rests on the DD-012 share register. The Disclosure Letter [10] itself admits this is just "the source relied on" and not Buyer verification.
- **Why it matters:** The register is an internal Company record, not independent proof of title.
- **Push back:** Require independent evidence of title, ownership, encumbrances and authority:
  - current ASIC company extract and historical allotment and transfer filings;
  - share certificates;
  - PPSR search against the Seller and the Company;
  - constitution and any shareholder agreement (pre-emption and drag rights);
  - Seller board resolutions authorising the sale.
- Combined with 1.4, title must sit in the Fundamental regime.

### 3.9 Lower-priority items: lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
These are not playbook items, but they should be confirmed:
- **Lease:** Confirm the DD-007 obligation is notification only, and add the notice as a Seller covenant.
- **Mossvale:** Confirm the DD-009 assignment restriction is not triggered by a share sale, with no change-of-control limb elsewhere in the contract.

The Seller's own wording is carefully hedged ("the material does not describe…"), so we should verify these against the source documents rather than rely on the letter.
